Why Streaming Matters

Waiting for a full batch before rendering anything makes a translation feature feel slow even when the total latency is unchanged. Users tolerate a slow answer far better when it arrives incrementally, and the first paragraph is what they actually look at.

The mechanism is straightforward: the model streams JSON, the server extracts each complete array element as soon as it closes, and the extension validates that element before rendering it. Nothing partial ever reaches the page, because a half-written object cannot be validated.

There is a subtlety worth calling out. Once items are written to the store as they arrive, a later failure no longer means the whole batch failed. Some items may already be on screen. Retrying the batch from scratch would re-translate them, wasting tokens and overwriting content the user is already reading.

The fix is to filter the retry payload down to the items that have not been delivered yet. That keeps retries cheap and keeps rendered output stable, at the cost of a slightly more involved bookkeeping step in the queue.

Streaming also changes how errors surface. A mid-stream failure produces a partial result plus an error, rather than a clean failure. The caller has to decide what to keep. Keeping what arrived is almost always the right call, since those items passed validation independently.

None of this is complicated, but all of it is easy to get subtly wrong. The tests that matter most are the ones that assert intermediate state rather than final state, because final state looks identical whether or not streaming actually happened.
